topics.title: The Periodic Table
topics.notesHtml:
The Periodic Table

The Periodic Table is a list of elements arranged in order of increasing proton (atomic) number. It consists of Periods and Groups.

Periods

  • Runs horizontally from left to right
  • Numbered 1–7
  • Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells
  • Period number = number of shells
  • Period 2: 2 shells (e.g. Li – 2,1; C – 2,4)
  • Period 3: 3 shells (e.g. Mg – 2,8,2; Si – 2,8,4)

Groups

  • Runs vertically from top to bottom
  • Numbered 1–18
  • Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons
  • Group number = number of valence electrons
  • Group 1: 1 valence electron (e.g. Li – 2,1; Na – 2,8,1)
  • Group 17/VII: 7 valence electrons (e.g. F – 2,7; Cl – 2,8,7)

Periods and Groups Summary

  • Periods: Period number corresponds to number of electron shells; same period, same number of shells, and vice versa.
  • Groups: Group number corresponds to number of valence electrons; same group, same number of valence electrons, and vice versa.

Period 3 Element Properties

Explanation: Elements in Groups I–III are metals and tend to lose electrons to form cations (+ve ions); charge of ion = group number. Elements in Groups IV and V share electrons to form covalent bonds instead of ions. Elements in Groups VI and VII are non-metals and tend to gain electrons to form anions (-ve ions). Elements in Group 0 have a stable electronic configuration and do not form compounds.

Physical Properties of Elements — Colour

Gases:

  • Brown: NO₂ (g), Br₂ (g)
  • Colourless: CO₂ (g), O₂ (g), SO₂ (g)
  • Yellowish-Green: Cl₂

Metals:

  • Reddish Brown: Cu (s)
  • Silvery: Ag, Fe, Mg, Zn, Ni, Cr, Al

Ions:

  • Blue: Cu²⁺ (aq)
  • Yellow: Fe³⁺ (aq)
  • Green: Fe²⁺ (aq); [Cr³⁺ (aq)]
  • Colourless: Mg²⁺, Na⁺, Pb²⁺, Al³⁺, Zn²⁺

Iodine:

  • I₂ (aq): brown; dissolves in alcohol/H₂O
  • I₂ (s): black
  • On heating (↓ sublimation), I₂ (g): purple

Note: Colours change as substances change from elements, to ions, to compounds. Example: Bismuth(III) Oxide is yellow while Bismuth metal is silver.

flashcards.q: What is the Periodic Table?
flashcards.a: A list of elements arranged in order of increasing proton (atomic) number, consisting of Periods and Groups.

flashcards.q: What does the period number correspond to?
flashcards.a: The number of electron shells in an atom of that element.

flashcards.q: What does the group number correspond to?
flashcards.a: The number of valence electrons in an atom of that element.

flashcards.q: How many shells does a Period 2 element have? Give an example.
flashcards.a: 2 shells; e.g. Li (2,1) or C (2,4).

flashcards.q: How many valence electrons does a Group 1 element have? Give an example.
flashcards.a: 1 valence electron; e.g. Li (2,1) or Na (2,8,1).

flashcards.q: In Period 3, which elements are metallic, metalloid, and non-metallic?
flashcards.a: Na and Mg are metallic; Al and Si are metalloid; P, S, Cl, Ar are non-metallic.

flashcards.q: What is the nature of the oxides of Group 1/2, Group 13/14, and Group 15-18 elements in Period 3?
flashcards.a: Group 1/2 oxides are alkali; Group 13/14 oxides are amphoteric; Group 15-17 oxides are acidic.

flashcards.q: What charge of ion do Group I, II, and III elements typically form?
flashcards.a: +1, +2, and +3 respectively, as they lose electrons to form cations.

flashcards.q: Why do Group IV and V elements not typically form simple ions?
flashcards.a: They tend to share electrons to form covalent bonds instead of ionic bonds.

flashcards.q: Why are Group 0 (18) elements unreactive and do not form compounds?
flashcards.a: They have a stable, full outer electron shell configuration.

flashcards.q: What colour is aqueous Cu²⁺ and Fe³⁺?
flashcards.a: Cu²⁺ (aq) is blue; Fe³⁺ (aq) is yellow.

flashcards.q: What colour is Cl₂ gas?
flashcards.a: Yellowish-green.

flashcards.q: Describe the appearance of iodine in solid, aqueous, and gaseous form.
flashcards.a: Solid I₂ is black, aqueous I₂ is brown, and gaseous I₂ (on sublimation) is purple.

flashcards.q: Name two properties of Group 1 metals.
flashcards.a: Soft and easily cut with shiny/silvery freshly-cut surface; low melting/boiling point; low density (potassium floats on water).

flashcards.q: Name two properties of transition metals.
flashcards.a: Good conductors of electricity; may form coloured compounds; high melting/boiling points and densities; form ions with different oxidation states.

quiz.question: What determines the period number of an element?
quiz.explanation: The period number corresponds to the number of electron shells an atom has.

quiz.question: Which Period 3 element is classified as a metalloid?
quiz.explanation: Silicon (Si) is classified as a metalloid, sharing properties of metals and non-metals.

quiz.question: What is the charge on ions formed by Group 17 elements?
quiz.explanation: Group 17 elements are non-metals that gain one electron to form -1 ions (e.g. F⁻, Cl⁻).

quiz.question: What colour is aqueous Fe²⁺?
quiz.explanation: According to the notes, Fe²⁺ (aq) is green.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT a property of Group 1 metals?
choices: Shiny and silvery when freshly cut
quiz.explanation: Group 1 metals have low density (e.g. potassium floats on water), unlike transition metals which have high densities.

quiz.question: What is the nature of the oxide formed by aluminium and silicon in Period 3?
quiz.explanation: Al and Si oxides are amphoteric, as noted in the Period 3 element properties table.

quiz.question: Why do noble gases not form compounds?
choices: They have a stable, full outer electron shell
They have too many valence electrons
quiz.explanation: Noble gases have a stable, full outer shell configuration, making them largely unreactive.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain why elements in the same group of the Periodic Table have similar chemical properties.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons. Since chemical properties are largely determined by valence electrons, elements in the same group react in similar ways.
rubric: States that group number = number of valence electrons
Links valence electrons to chemical properties/reactivity
Gives or implies an example (e.g. Group 1 or Group 17)

shortAnswer.prompt: Describe the trend in ion charge formed across Period 3, from Group I to Group VII, and explain why.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Group I, II and III elements form +1, +2 and +3 ions respectively as they are metals that lose electrons equal to their group number. Group IV and V elements tend to form covalent bonds rather than simple ions. Group VI and VII elements are non-metals that gain electrons to form -2 and -1 ions respectively. Group 0 elements do not form ions as they already have a stable electron configuration.
rubric: Correctly states +1/+2/+3 for Groups I-III
Notes Groups IV/V form covalent bonds instead of ions
Correctly states -2/-1 for Groups VI/VII
Explains Group 0 unreactivity

topics.title: Periodic Trends: Atomic and Ionic Radii
topics.notesHtml:
1. Atomic and Ionic Radii

General Trend: (Note: Arrowheads point towards the direction where the value increases/is larger.)

  • Down Groups 1 and 17: atomic and ionic radii increase.
  • Across Period 3: atomic and ionic radii decrease.

flashcards.q: What happens to atomic and ionic radii down Groups 1 and 17?
flashcards.a: They increase.

flashcards.q: What happens to atomic and ionic radii across Period 3?
flashcards.a: They decrease.

flashcards.q: Why does atomic radius increase down a group?
flashcards.a: More electron shells are added down the group, increasing the distance between the nucleus and outer electrons.

flashcards.q: Does atomic radius across Period 3 increase or decrease from Na to Cl?
flashcards.a: It decreases.

flashcards.q: What is the general trend indicated by the arrowhead direction in these diagrams?
flashcards.a: The arrowhead points towards the direction where the value increases/is larger.

flashcards.q: Which two groups are used to illustrate the down-group trend in atomic/ionic radii?
flashcards.a: Group 1 and Group 17.

flashcards.q: Is the atomic radius trend across a period the same or different from the trend down a group?
flashcards.a: Different — down a group radii increase, across a period radii decrease.

flashcards.q: What structural feature causes radii to decrease across Period 3?
flashcards.a: An increase in nuclear charge without addition of new electron shells, pulling electrons closer to the nucleus.

quiz.question: What happens to atomic radius down Group 1?
quiz.explanation: Atomic and ionic radii increase down Groups 1 and 17.

quiz.question: What happens to atomic radius across Period 3 (left to right)?
quiz.explanation: Atomic and ionic radii decrease across Period 3.

quiz.question: Which of the following elements would have the largest atomic radius: Na, Mg, Al, or Si?
quiz.explanation: Radii decrease across Period 3, so Na (leftmost, Group 1) has the largest atomic radius.

quiz.question: Which group's ionic radius trend is described alongside Group 1 in the notes?
quiz.explanation: The notes specifically describe atomic and ionic radii trends down Groups 1 and 17.

quiz.question: Comparing Li and K (both Group 1), which has a larger atomic radius?
quiz.explanation: Atomic radius increases down Group 1, so K (further down) is larger than Li.

shortAnswer.prompt: State and explain the general trend in atomic radii down Group 17.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Atomic radii increase down Group 17. This is because elements further down the group have more electron shells, increasing the distance between the nucleus and the valence electrons.
rubric: States radii increase down the group
Provides reasoning based on number of electron shells

shortAnswer.prompt: Compare the general trend of atomic radii down a group versus across Period 3.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Down a group (e.g. Group 1 or 17), atomic and ionic radii increase due to additional electron shells. Across Period 3, atomic and ionic radii decrease from left to right.
rubric: Correctly identifies down-group trend as increasing
Correctly identifies across-period trend as decreasing

topics.title: Periodic Trends: Melting/Boiling Points
topics.notesHtml:
2. Melting/Boiling Points

Down Groups 1 and 17

Group 1 and Group 17 elements show opposite trends in melting/boiling point down the group.

Across Period 3

Metals: Melting/boiling points generally increase across the metallic elements of Period 3.

Silicon: Silicon is a metalloid (shares some properties of metals and non-metals). Si has a giant covalent structure similar to diamond (each atom is bonded to 4 others in a tetrahedral arrangement). All Si atoms are held together by strong covalent bonds, which require a large amount of heat energy to overcome. As a result, its melting point/boiling point is very high.

Non-metals: Melting/boiling points of the non-metals in Period 3 are generally low, as they exist as simple molecular structures held together by weak intermolecular forces.

flashcards.q: What is the general trend in melting/boiling point down Groups 1 and 17?
flashcards.a: Group 1 and Group 17 elements show opposite trends in melting/boiling point down the group.

flashcards.q: What is the trend in melting/boiling point across the metallic elements of Period 3?
flashcards.a: Melting/boiling points generally increase across the metallic elements of Period 3.

flashcards.q: Why does silicon have a very high melting/boiling point?
flashcards.a: Silicon has a giant covalent structure (like diamond) where each atom bonds to 4 others in a tetrahedral arrangement, held together by strong covalent bonds requiring large amounts of energy to break.

flashcards.q: What structure does silicon share similarities with?
flashcards.a: Diamond.

flashcards.q: How many other atoms is each silicon atom bonded to in its structure?
flashcards.a: 4, in a tetrahedral arrangement.

flashcards.q: What type of bonds hold silicon atoms together?
flashcards.a: Strong covalent bonds.

flashcards.q: What is the general trend in melting/boiling points of the non-metals in Period 3?
flashcards.a: They are generally low.

flashcards.q: Why are the melting/boiling points of Period 3 non-metals low?
flashcards.a: They exist as simple molecular structures held together by weak intermolecular forces.

flashcards.q: What kind of structure is silicon classified as?
flashcards.a: A metalloid with a giant covalent structure.

quiz.question: Why does silicon have a very high melting point compared to other Period 3 non-metals?
choices: It has a small atomic radius
It has a giant covalent structure with strong covalent bonds
quiz.explanation: Silicon has a giant covalent structure similar to diamond, requiring large amounts of energy to break the strong covalent bonds.

quiz.question: What is the general trend of melting/boiling points across the non-metals of Period 3?
quiz.explanation: Non-metals in Period 3 have simple molecular structures with weak intermolecular forces, giving low melting/boiling points.

quiz.question: What describes the melting/boiling point trend down Group 1 compared to Group 17?
quiz.explanation: The notes state Group 1 and Group 17 elements show opposite trends in melting/boiling point down the group.

quiz.question: How many silicon atoms is each silicon atom bonded to in its giant covalent structure?
quiz.explanation: Each Si atom is bonded to 4 others in a tetrahedral arrangement.

quiz.question: What holds simple molecular non-metal structures together in Period 3?
quiz.explanation: Non-metals exist as simple molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces, giving low melting/boiling points.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain why silicon has an unusually high melting point compared to other elements in Period 3.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Silicon has a giant covalent structure similar to diamond, where each Si atom is bonded to 4 other atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement via strong covalent bonds. A large amount of energy is required to overcome these strong bonds, giving silicon a very high melting/boiling point.
rubric: Mentions giant covalent structure similar to diamond
States each atom bonds to 4 others tetrahedrally
States strong covalent bonds require large energy to break
Concludes with high melting/boiling point

shortAnswer.prompt: Describe and explain the melting/boiling point trend of non-metals in Period 3.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The melting/boiling points of non-metals in Period 3 are generally low because they exist as simple molecular structures held together by weak intermolecular forces, which require little energy to overcome.
rubric: States melting/boiling points are generally low
Explains via simple molecular structure
Explains via weak intermolecular forces

topics.title: Periodic Trends: First Ionization Energy
topics.notesHtml:
3. First Ionization Energy

Defined as the minimum energy required to remove an electron from a neutral atom (in its gaseous state).

General Trend

  • Down Groups 1 and 17: first ionization energy decreases (atomic radius increases, outer electrons further from nucleus and more shielded, easier to remove).
  • Across Period 3: first ionization energy generally increases (atomic radius decreases, nuclear charge increases, electrons held more strongly).

flashcards.q: Define first ionization energy.
flashcards.a: The minimum energy required to remove an electron from a neutral atom in its gaseous state.

flashcards.q: What happens to first ionization energy down Groups 1 and 17?
flashcards.a: It decreases.

flashcards.q: Why does first ionization energy decrease down a group?
flashcards.a: Atomic radius increases, so outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, making them easier to remove.

flashcards.q: What happens to first ionization energy across Period 3?
flashcards.a: It generally increases.

flashcards.q: Why does first ionization energy increase across Period 3?
flashcards.a: Atomic radius decreases and nuclear charge increases, so electrons are held more strongly.

flashcards.q: What state must the atom be in for first ionization energy to be measured?
flashcards.a: Gaseous state.

flashcards.q: How is atomic radius related to first ionization energy down a group?
flashcards.a: As atomic radius increases down a group, first ionization energy decreases.

flashcards.q: How is nuclear charge related to first ionization energy across a period?
flashcards.a: As nuclear charge increases across a period, first ionization energy generally increases.

quiz.question: What is the definition of first ionization energy?
choices: The energy released when a compound forms
The energy needed to break a covalent bond
The energy released when an atom gains an electron
The minimum energy required to remove an electron from a neutral gaseous atom
quiz.explanation: First ionization energy is defined as the minimum energy required to remove an electron from a neutral atom in the gaseous state.

quiz.question: What happens to first ionization energy down Group 1?
quiz.explanation: Down Group 1, atomic radius increases and outer electrons are more shielded, so ionization energy decreases.

quiz.question: What happens to first ionization energy across Period 3, from Na to Ar?
quiz.explanation: Across Period 3, atomic radius decreases and nuclear charge increases, so first ionization energy generally increases.

quiz.question: Why is it easier to remove an electron from K than from Na?
choices: K's outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded
K has a smaller atomic radius
K has a higher nuclear charge effect on outer electrons
quiz.explanation: K is further down Group 1, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, requiring less energy to remove.

quiz.question: Which factor explains increasing ionization energy across Period 3?
choices: Increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic radius
quiz.explanation: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while atomic radius decreases, holding electrons more strongly and increasing ionization energy.

shortAnswer.prompt: Define first ionization energy and explain why it decreases down Group 17.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: First ionization energy is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from a neutral gaseous atom. Down Group 17, atomic radius increases due to additional electron shells, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded from its attractive force, making them easier to remove and lowering the ionization energy.
rubric: Correct definition of first ionization energy
States atomic radius increases down the group
Links increased radius/shielding to easier electron removal
Concludes ionization energy decreases

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain why first ionization energy generally increases across Period 3.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Across Period 3, the atomic radius decreases while the nuclear charge increases. This means the outer electrons are held more strongly by the nucleus, requiring more energy to remove them, so first ionization energy generally increases.
rubric: States atomic radius decreases across the period
States nuclear charge increases across the period
Links these to electrons being held more strongly
Concludes ionization energy increases

topics.title: Periodic Trends: Reactivity
topics.notesHtml:
4. Reactivity

Defined as how readily a substance undergoes a chemical reaction; can be classified according to its affinity to lose or gain electrons.

General Trend

  • Down Groups 1 and 17: reactivity trends differ by group (Group 1 metals become more reactive going down; Group 17 non-metals become less reactive going down).
  • Across Period 3: reactivity of metals decreases while, among the non-metals, reactivity trends are related to ease of gaining electrons.

Noble Gases

Noble gases (Group 18/0) are largely unreactive due to their stable, full outer electron shells.

flashcards.q: How is reactivity defined?
flashcards.a: How readily a substance undergoes a chemical reaction; can be classified according to its affinity to lose or gain electrons.

flashcards.q: What happens to reactivity of Group 1 metals down the group?
flashcards.a: They become more reactive going down.

flashcards.q: What happens to reactivity of Group 17 non-metals down the group?
flashcards.a: They become less reactive going down.

flashcards.q: What happens to the reactivity of metals across Period 3?
flashcards.a: It decreases.

flashcards.q: Among non-metals in Period 3, what is reactivity related to?
flashcards.a: Ease of gaining electrons.

flashcards.q: Why are noble gases largely unreactive?
flashcards.a: Because of their stable, full outer electron shells.

flashcards.q: Which group of elements has a reactivity trend opposite to Group 1 down the group?
flashcards.a: Group 17 — Group 1 becomes more reactive going down while Group 17 becomes less reactive going down.

flashcards.q: What group number are noble gases in?
flashcards.a: Group 18 (or Group 0).

quiz.question: How does reactivity change down Group 1?
quiz.explanation: Group 1 metals become more reactive going down the group.

quiz.question: How does reactivity change down Group 17?
quiz.explanation: Group 17 non-metals become less reactive going down the group.

quiz.question: What best describes reactivity?
choices: The melting point of a substance
How readily a substance undergoes a chemical reaction
The colour change of a substance
quiz.explanation: Reactivity is defined as how readily a substance undergoes a chemical reaction.

quiz.question: Why are noble gases largely unreactive?
choices: They are always in liquid form
They have very high atomic mass
They have stable, full outer electron shells
quiz.explanation: Noble gases have stable, full outer electron shells, making them largely unreactive.

quiz.question: What happens to the reactivity of metals across Period 3?
quiz.explanation: According to the notes, reactivity of metals decreases across Period 3.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain why Group 1 and Group 17 elements show opposite reactivity trends down their respective groups.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Group 1 metals react by losing electrons; going down the group, atomic radius increases and outer electrons are more easily lost, so reactivity increases. Group 17 non-metals react by gaining electrons; going down the group, atomic radius increases making it harder to attract and gain an additional electron, so reactivity decreases.
rubric: States Group 1 reactivity increases down the group
States Group 17 reactivity decreases down the group
Explains reactivity in terms of losing (Group 1) or gaining (Group 17) electrons

shortAnswer.prompt: Why are noble gases largely unreactive?
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Noble gases have stable, full outer electron shells, so they have little tendency to lose, gain, or share electrons, making them largely unreactive.
rubric: States noble gases have full/stable outer shells
Links this to lack of reactivity

topics.title: Metals and Alloys
topics.notesHtml:
Metals and Alloys

Properties of Metals

PropertyReason
Good conductors of heat and electricityMobile electrons act as charge carriers and aid in conduction
High densities, melting points and boiling points (exception of Group 1 metals)Strong electrostatic forces of attraction hold metal ions closely together, so more ions occupy less space and a larger amount of energy is required to break the bonds
Malleable and ductileThe 'sea of electrons' still holds the metal ions together, even after distortion
Pure metals are too soft (thus not widely used in industry)—
Pure metals may react with air and water, thus wearing away or corroding easily (thus not widely used in industry)—

Alloys

Alloy: a mixture of a metal with one or a few other elements (metal or non-metal).

Property of AlloysExample / Reason
Alloys make metals harder and strongerBrass, an alloy of copper and zinc, is harder and stronger than pure zinc. Atoms of the added element have a different size, disrupting the orderly arrangement of atoms so that atoms cannot slide over each other easily when a force is applied.
Alloys improve the appearance of metalsPewter — an alloy of tin, antimony and copper — looks better than tin, which is duller in comparison.
Alloys lower the melting point of metalsSolder is an alloy of tin and lead; it has a lower melting point than pure tin or lead and is used for joining metals.
Alloys make metals more resistant to corrosionCupronickel is an alloy of copper and nickel; it is used in coins as it does not corrode easily.

flashcards.q: Why are metals good conductors of heat and electricity?
flashcards.a: Mobile electrons act as charge carriers and aid in conduction.

flashcards.q: Why do metals (except Group 1) have high densities, melting and boiling points?
flashcards.a: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction hold metal ions closely together, so more ions occupy less space and more energy is needed to break the bonds.

flashcards.q: Why are metals malleable and ductile?
flashcards.a: The 'sea of electrons' still holds the metal ions together, even after distortion.

flashcards.q: Why are pure metals often not used in industry?
flashcards.a: They are too soft, and may react with air and water, corroding easily.

flashcards.q: Define an alloy.
flashcards.a: A mixture of a metal with one or a few other elements (metal or non-metal).

flashcards.q: How do alloys make metals harder and stronger? Give an example.
flashcards.a: Atoms of the added element have a different size, disrupting the orderly arrangement so atoms cannot slide over each other easily; e.g. brass (copper + zinc) is harder and stronger than pure zinc.

flashcards.q: Give an example of an alloy that improves the appearance of a metal.
flashcards.a: Pewter (tin, antimony, copper) looks better than tin, which is duller.

flashcards.q: Give an example of an alloy that lowers the melting point of metals.
flashcards.a: Solder (tin and lead) has a lower melting point than pure tin or lead and is used for joining metals.

flashcards.q: Give an example of an alloy that resists corrosion.
flashcards.a: Cupronickel (copper and nickel) is used in coins as it does not corrode easily.

flashcards.q: What are the components of brass?
flashcards.a: Copper and zinc.

flashcards.q: What are the components of pewter?
flashcards.a: Tin, antimony and copper.

flashcards.q: What are the components of solder?
flashcards.a: Tin and lead.

quiz.question: Why are metals good conductors of electricity?
choices: They have a giant covalent structure
Mobile electrons act as charge carriers
quiz.explanation: Mobile electrons in metals act as charge carriers, allowing conduction of electricity.

quiz.question: What is an alloy?
choices: A mixture of a metal with one or a few other elements
quiz.explanation: An alloy is defined as a mixture of a metal with one or a few other elements (metal or non-metal).

quiz.question: Why does alloying make a metal harder and stronger, as in brass?
choices: It increases the metal's melting point always
Different-sized atoms disrupt the orderly arrangement, preventing layers from sliding easily
It removes the metallic bond entirely
It removes electrons from the metal
quiz.explanation: Atoms of the added element have a different size, disrupting the orderly arrangement of atoms so they cannot slide over each other easily.

quiz.question: Which alloy is used for joining metals due to its lower melting point?
quiz.explanation: Solder, an alloy of tin and lead, has a lower melting point and is used for joining metals.

quiz.question: Which alloy is used in coins because it resists corrosion?
quiz.explanation: Cupronickel, an alloy of copper and nickel, is used in coins as it does not corrode easily.

quiz.question: Why are pure metals malleable and ductile?
choices: Because their ions are fixed in place
Because the sea of electrons still holds ions together even after distortion
Because they have low melting points
quiz.explanation: The sea of mobile electrons continues to hold the metal ions together even when the metal is distorted, allowing malleability and ductility.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain why pure metals are generally too soft for industrial use, and how alloying addresses this.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Pure metals have an orderly arrangement of identically-sized atoms that can slide over each other easily when a force is applied, making them soft. Alloying introduces atoms of a different size, which disrupts this orderly arrangement so that the layers of atoms cannot slide over each other as easily, making the alloy harder and stronger than the pure metal (e.g. brass is harder than pure zinc).
rubric: Explains why pure metals are soft (orderly, same-sized atoms slide easily)
Explains how different-sized alloying atoms disrupt this arrangement
Gives a correct example, e.g. brass and zinc

shortAnswer.prompt: Using suitable examples, explain three advantages of using alloys instead of pure metals.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Alloys can be harder and stronger, such as brass (copper and zinc) being harder than pure zinc. Alloys can improve appearance, such as pewter (tin, antimony, copper) looking better than dull tin. Alloys can lower melting point, such as solder (tin and lead), useful for joining metals. Alloys can also improve corrosion resistance, such as cupronickel (copper and nickel) used in coins.
rubric: Names at least three distinct advantages of alloying
Provides correct alloy examples for each advantage
Correctly names the constituent metals of each alloy example

Copper (Cu)Forms basic oxide CuO
Silver (Ag)Forms basic oxide Ag₂O
Gold (Au)Forms basic oxide Au₂O₃

Reaction with Cold Water

General equation: Metal (s) + H₂O (l) → Metal Hydroxide (aq) + H₂ (g)

Note: A metal hydroxide is formed instead of an oxide as the oxide of these metals all react with water to produce a hydroxide (recall Acids and Alkalis).

MetalObservations
Potassium (K)Very violent reaction; sparks formed; metal darts on water surface; highly exothermic; hydrogen gas explodes with a lilac flame; forms effervescence. Forms alkali KOH + H₂.
Sodium (Na)Violent reaction; sparks formed; metal darts on water surface; highly exothermic; hydrogen gas explodes with a yellow flame; forms effervescence. Forms alkali NaOH + H₂.
Calcium (Ca)Fast reaction; sinks in water (denser); forms effervescence. Forms alkali Ca(OH)₂ + H₂.
Magnesium (Mg)Slow reaction; forms some effervescence. Forms base Mg(OH)₂ + H₂.
Aluminium (Al), Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe), Lead (Pb), Copper (Cu), Silver (Ag), Gold (Au)Do not react with cold water.

Reaction with Steam

General equation: Metal (s) + H₂O (g) → Metal Oxide (s) + H₂ (g)

Method: The metal and water in glass wool is heated strongly, turning the water into steam. Occasionally move the Bunsen burner to the glass wool to increase the steam flow. Test the gas collected with a lighted splint to ensure hydrogen is collected.

Note: Bubbles observed during the experiment are not enough to prove that a reaction took place, as steam will force air to rise through the water. A flame may be lit in order to confirm the hydrogen gas produced during the reaction.

MetalObservations
Potassium (K)Very explosive reaction. Forms oxide K₂O + H₂.
Sodium (Na)Violent reaction. Forms oxide Na₂O + H₂.
Calcium (Ca)Very fast reaction. Forms oxide CaO + H₂.
Magnesium (Mg)Fast reaction; produces a white glow. Forms oxide MgO + H₂.
Aluminium (Al)No reaction, due to the unreactive aluminium oxide layer.
Zinc (Zn)Reacts readily. Forms oxide ZnO (hot: yellow, cold: white) + H₂.
Iron (Fe)Reacts slowly. Forms Fe₃O₄ + H₂.
Lead (Pb), Copper (Cu), Silver (Ag), Gold (Au)Do not react with steam.

Hydrogen (H): If a metal is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, it should, in principle, be able to remove the oxygen from water to leave hydrogen gas. Metals below hydrogen won't be able to react with water in this way (exception of Pb).

Reaction with Dilute Acid

General equations: Metal (s) + HCl (aq) → Metal Chloride (aq) + H₂ (g); Metal (s) + H₂SO₄ (aq) → Metal Sulfate (aq) + H₂ (g)

MetalObservations
Potassium (K) — most reactiveVery explosive reaction. Forms salt KCl + H₂.
Sodium (Na)Very explosive reaction. Forms salt NaCl + H₂.
Calcium (Ca)Violent reaction. Forms salt CaCl₂ + H₂.
Magnesium (Mg)Rapid reaction. Forms salt MgCl₂ + H₂.
Aluminium (Al)Slow reaction, due to the aluminium oxide layer.
Zinc (Zn)Reacts moderately fast. Forms salt ZnCl₂ + H₂.
Iron (Fe)Reacts slowly. Forms salt FeCl₂ + H₂.
Lead (Pb)No noticeable reaction with either sulfuric or hydrochloric acid, as an insoluble layer of salt (PbSO₄/PbCl₂) forms.
Copper (Cu), Silver (Ag), Gold (Au)Do not react with acid.

Hydrogen (H): Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with acids; those below hydrogen don't. Of the metals above hydrogen, reactivity increases the further up the reactivity series you go.

Decomposition of Metal Nitrates/Carbonates

General equations: Metal Nitrate (s) --heat--> Metal Oxide (s) + NO₂ (g) + O₂ (g); Metal Carbonate (s) --heat--> Metal Oxide (s) + CO₂ (g)

MetalStability
Potassium (K), Sodium (Na)Very stable; do not decompose.
Calcium (Ca), Magnesium (Mg), Aluminium (Al), Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe), Lead (Pb), Copper (Cu)Unstable; decompose to form oxide + CO₂/NO₂ + O₂.
Silver (Ag), Gold (Au)Unstable; decompose to form the metal itself + CO₂/NO₂ + O₂.

Metal Reduction Methods

Electrolysis: Metal Oxide → Metal + O₂. Carbon Reduction: Metal Oxide + CO → Metal + CO₂.

MetalExtraction Method
Potassium (K), Sodium (Na), Calcium (Ca), Magnesium (Mg), Aluminium (Al)Electrolysis
Carbon (C)Metals above carbon are more reactive and cannot be displaced by carbon, so electrolysis is used instead to extract the pure metal. Metals below carbon are less reactive and can be displaced by carbon.
Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe), Lead (Pb), Copper (Cu), Silver (Ag), Gold (Au)Reduction with carbon

Uses of the Reactivity Series

Metals lose electrons to form positive ions (cations). The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions — a more reactive metal has a greater tendency to form positive ions.

Displacement Reactions Between Metals

Displacement of Metal: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

Example: Adding Fe to a solution of CuSO₄: Fe (s) + CuSO₄ (aq) → FeSO₄ (aq) + Cu (s). Iron is more reactive than copper as it is above copper in the reactivity series. Hence iron can displace copper from copper(II) sulfate solution.

Observations (write only what is seen, as a change from before to after):

  • Fe decreases in size (Fe becomes Fe²⁺ ions)
  • Solution turns from blue to green (blue Cu²⁺ ions replaced by green Fe²⁺ ions)
  • Reddish-brown copper metal forms at the bottom (Cu²⁺ ions become Cu)

Example: Adding Cu to a solution of FeSO₄: Copper is less reactive than iron as it is below iron in the reactivity series. Hence copper cannot displace iron from iron(II) sulfate solution.

Metal and Oxide of Another Metal Reaction

A more reactive metal can reduce the oxide of a less reactive metal.

Example: The magnesium ribbon acts as a fuse. When ignited, it provides enough energy to start the reaction between zinc and copper(II) oxide to form zinc oxide and copper: Zn (s) + CuO (s) --heat--> ZnO (s) + Cu (s). Zinc is more reactive than copper — it forms Zn²⁺ ions more readily — and copper(II) oxide is reduced to copper.

topics.title: Reduction and Oxidation (Redox)
topics.notesHtml:
Reduction and Oxidation

In the Reactivity Series, we learnt about displacement reactions. These fall under a larger classification known as Redox (Reduction–Oxidation) reactions.

Identifying Redox Reactions

Example reactions: CuO + Mg → MgO + Cu, and H₂S + Cl → 2HCl + S

BasisOxidationReduction
Oxygen transferMg is oxidised as it gains O to form MgO. Oxidation is gain of oxygen.CuO is reduced as it loses O to form Cu. Reduction is loss of oxygen.
Electron transferIn Cu²⁺ + Mg → Cu + Mg²⁺: Mg loses 2 electrons per atom to form Mg²⁺ ions; Mg has been oxidised to Mg²⁺. Oxidation is loss of electrons.In Cu²⁺ + Mg → Cu + Mg²⁺: Cu²⁺ gains 2 electrons per ion to form Cu; Cu²⁺ has been reduced to Cu. Reduction is gain of electrons.
Hydrogen transferH₂S is oxidised as it loses 2H to form S. Oxidation is loss of hydrogen.Cl is reduced as it gains 2H to form 2HCl. Reduction is gain of hydrogen.
Change in oxidation stateH₂S is oxidised as the oxidation state of S increases from -2 in H₂S to 0 in S. Oxidation is a gain (increase) in oxidation state.Cl is reduced as the oxidation state of Cl decreases from 0 in Cl to -1 in HCl. Reduction is a loss (decrease) in oxidation state.

Generally: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons), except when involving oxygen or oxidation state, where the opposite occurs (oxidation is a gain of oxygen/oxidation state; reduction is a loss of oxygen/oxidation state).

Oxidation and reduction always go hand-in-hand: if something is being oxidised, something else must be being reduced. A reaction in which both oxidation and reduction occur is called a redox reaction.

Examples of redox reactions: Electrolysis decomposition, Displacement reactions, Thermal decomposition.

Non-redox reactions: Neutralisation, Precipitation.

topics.title: Oxidation State
topics.notesHtml:
Oxidation State

Oxidation state: the charge an atom of an element would have if it existed as an ion in a compound. Even in a covalently-bonded compound, oxidation state applies. When a substance loses or gains electrons, its oxidation state changes.

[Oxidation state shows the total number of electrons which have been removed from an element (a positive oxidation state) or added to an element (a negative oxidation state) to get to its present state.]

CaseOxidation Number
Free, uncombined element (e.g. Cu, Mg, O₂, Cl₂, S₈, C, Si)0
Simple ion (e.g. Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, O²⁻, Cl⁻)Same as charge on ion (including +ve/-ve sign)
Group 1 metals in compounds (e.g. Na in NaCl, Na₂O; K in K₂O, KCl)+1
Group 2 metals in compounds (e.g. Mg in MgCl₂, MgO; Ca in CaO)+2
Hydrogen in most* compounds (e.g. H₂O, HCl, CH₄)+1
Oxygen in most** compounds (e.g. Na₂O, MgO, CO₂)-2
Fluorine (e.g. KF, MgF₂, HF)-1
Chlorine in most*** compounds (e.g. HCl, KCl, MgCl₂)-1
Sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms/ions in a compound (e.g. MgCl₂: Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻: +2 + 2(-1) = 0)0
Sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms in a polyatomic ion (e.g. SO₄²⁻: S + 4(-2) = -2, so S = -2 + 8 = +6)Same as the charge of the ion

Notes

  • * In metal hydrides, hydrogen is present as the hydride ion, H⁻, and thus has oxidation state -1.
  • ** In peroxides such as H₂O₂, each oxygen atom has oxidation state -1; in F₂O, fluorine is more electronegative and oxygen instead has oxidation state +2.
  • *** In compounds with F and O, Cl does not have oxidation state -1 (e.g. in ClO₃⁻, Cl has oxidation state +5).

topics.title: Electrolysis: Basics and Setup
topics.notesHtml:
Electrolysis

Electrolysis: the process of using electricity to break down or decompose a compound (usually an ionic compound in the molten state or in aqueous solution). Electrolysis takes place in an electrolytic cell.

Components of an Electrolytic Cell

  1. Battery: acts as an electron pump, drawing electrons away from the anode and towards the cathode.
  2. Electrodes: conduct electricity. Usually carbon (graphite) rods or metal plates, as they are inert and prevent reactions between the product and the electrodes.
    • Anode (+ve): connected to the positive terminal of the battery; it is the positive electrode and negative ions move towards it.
    • Cathode (-ve): connected to the negative terminal of the battery; it is the negative electrode and positive ions move towards it.
  3. Electrolyte: contains free-moving ions that allow electricity to flow through it. It is a molten ionic compound or an aqueous solution, and is decomposed to form cations and anions. Non-electrolytes are substances that do not conduct electricity under any conditions (e.g. sulfur, sugar, distilled water, ethanol).

During Electrolysis

  1. Electrons flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the battery.
  2. Flow of ions towards the electrodes constitutes the flow of electric current through the electrolyte.
  3. Anions move to the anode (+ve), giving up electrons at the anode as oxidation occurs [AnOx].
  4. Cations move to the cathode (-ve), receiving electrons at the cathode as reduction occurs [RedCat].

When cations or anions gain or lose electrons to form atoms or molecules, we say the cations or anions are discharged.

Solid, Molten and Aqueous States

Solid StateMolten StateAqueous State
Ions are held in fixed positions and cannot conduct electricity. No current flows through the circuit and no products are formed at the electrodes.Mobile ions are present, which carry charges and conduct electricity. Current flows through the circuit and products are formed at the electrodes.Mobile ions are present, which carry charges and conduct electricity. Current flows through the circuit and products are formed at the electrodes.

Note: The main difference between compounds in a molten state and an aqueous state for electrolysis is that compounds in a molten state do not have water (H⁺ and OH⁻ ions are not present), while compounds in an aqueous state do have water (H⁺ and OH⁻ ions are present).

Ionic Half Equations

Overall equation for electrolysis of molten sodium chloride: 2NaCl (l) → 2Na (l) + Cl₂ (g). Two redox reactions take place at each electrode, each forming a product:

Cathode: Na⁺ (l) + e⁻ → Na (l) [simplified]; 2Na⁺ (l) + 2e⁻ → 2Na (l) [corrected molar ratio]

Anode: 2Cl⁻ (l) → Cl₂ (g) + 2e⁻

Notes on Writing Half Equations
  • Ensure the number of atoms (here, Cl) match on both sides of the equation before determining the number of electrons.
  • Never subtract electrons — instead add them on the other side of the equation.
  • Charges on either side of the equation should add up to the same total charge.
  • When doing calculations, ensure the number of electrons in both half-equations are equal.
  • Losing electrons is written on the right (after the arrow); gaining electrons is written on the left (before the arrow). [Oxidation is loss (OIL), so written on the right after the arrow; Reduction is gain (RIG), so written on the left before the arrow.]
  • State symbols are required.

Electrolysis of Molten Compounds

A binary compound consists of two elements, usually a metal cation and a non-metal anion (e.g. NaCl, PbBr₂). In the electrolysis of molten binary compounds, the reactions and products are very straightforward.

At the anode: Negatively charged Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the anode and lose electrons to form chlorine gas. They are oxidised (OILoss) and the Cl⁻ ions are discharged: 2Cl⁻ (l) → Cl₂ (g) + 2e⁻

At the cathode: Positively charged Na⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode and each gain one electron to form a sodium atom. They are reduced (RIGain) and the Na⁺ ion is discharged: Na⁺ (l) + e⁻ → Na (l)

topics.title: Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions
topics.notesHtml:
Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions of Compounds

In an aqueous solution, multiple types of cations and anions are present. The products formed (if electrodes are inert) depend on: (i) selective discharge of anions (at the anode); (ii) selective discharge of cations (at the cathode); (iii) the effect of concentration on selective discharge of anions.

At the Cathode

H⁺ ions are selectively discharged in preference to ions of metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Metals below hydrogen (Cu, Ag) are discharged in preference to H⁺.

Note: Even if a metal is slightly above hydrogen, it can be selectively discharged through industrial means. In general, if a question states that electroplating is taking place, then it can be assumed that said metal is discharged (e.g. nickel).

At the Anode

Polyatomic ions (SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻) cannot be discharged and thus remain in the solution.

OH⁻ ions give up electrons most readily during electrolysis to form H₂O and O₂: 4OH⁻ (aq) → 2H₂O (l) + O₂ (g) + 4e⁻

In a solution with a concentrated halide solution (e.g. concentrated NaCl, KI), halide ions are more concentrated than OH⁻ ions and are selectively discharged in preference to OH⁻.

General Rules for Predicting Products of Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions

  1. Read the question for given information (concentrated/dilute? electroplating taking place?)
  2. Identify and list the cations and anions in the given electrolyte.
  3. Determine the anion that is discharged at the anode.
  4. Determine the cation that is discharged at the cathode.
  5. Identify the cations and anions that remain in solution after electrolysis — they form the product.

Electrolysis of Dilute Sodium Chloride Solution

Ions present: Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺, OH⁻

At the cathode: Na⁺ and H⁺ are present. H⁺ is selectively discharged as H₂ gas: 2H⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂ (g). Na⁺ ions remain in solution.

At the anode: Cl⁻ and OH⁻ are present (note: dilute). OH⁻ is selectively discharged as O₂ gas: 4OH⁻ (aq) → 2H₂O (l) + O₂ (g) + 4e⁻. Cl⁻ ions remain in solution.

Overall reaction: 2H₂O (l) → 2H₂ (g) + O₂ (g), which is essentially the electrolysis of water.

Notes:

  • For every mole of O₂ produced, twice the moles of H₂ is produced.
  • Even less O₂ may be collected as it dissolves slightly in water.
  • For electrolysis of pure water, a small amount of ionic compound (or H₂SO₄) is added to electrolyse the water.

Electrolysis of Concentrated Sodium Chloride Solution

Ions present: Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺, OH⁻

At the cathode: Na⁺ and H⁺ are present. H⁺ is selectively discharged as H₂ gas: 2H⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂ (g). Na⁺ ions remain in solution.

At the anode: Cl⁻ and OH⁻ are present (note: concentrated Cl⁻). Cl⁻ is selectively discharged as Cl₂ gas: 2Cl⁻ (aq) → Cl₂ (g) + 2e⁻. OH⁻ ions remain in solution.

Overall reaction: Equal volumes of Cl₂ and H₂ gases are produced. The remaining Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions recombine to form NaOH, so the solution turns alkaline. Litmus paper at the anode is bleached by Cl₂; litmus paper in the solution turns from red to blue.

Electrolysis of Aqueous Copper Sulfate Solution (Inert Electrodes)

Ions present: Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻

At the cathode: Cu²⁺ and H⁺ are present. Cu²⁺ is selectively discharged as Cu, since Cu is below H in the reactivity series: Cu²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu (s). A copper coating forms around the cathode. H⁺ ions remain in the solution (Cathode – Coating).

At the anode: SO₄²⁻ and OH⁻ are present. OH⁻ is selectively discharged as O₂ gas: 4OH⁻ (aq) → 2H₂O (l) + O₂ (g) + 4e⁻. SO₄²⁻ ions remain in solution.

O₂ gas is produced at the anode while copper is deposited at the cathode. The blue colour fades as the concentration of Cu²⁺ ions decreases. The solution becomes acidic as the remaining H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ recombine to form H₂SO₄ (sulfuric acid).

Electrolysis of Aqueous Copper Sulfate Solution (with Copper Electrodes)

Ions present: Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻

At the cathode: Cu²⁺ and H⁺ are present. Cu²⁺ is selectively discharged as Cu, since Cu is below H in the reactivity series: Cu²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu (s). The copper cathode increases in size.

At the anode: SO₄²⁻ and OH⁻ are present. Since Cu is not inert, the anode dissolves (oxidises): Cu (s) → Cu²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻. The copper anode decreases in size.

For every mole of Cu²⁺ discharged at the cathode, 1 mole of Cu²⁺ is produced at the anode, so there is no net loss of Cu²⁺ ions from the solution. The colour and concentration of CuSO₄ remain unchanged.

topics.title: Applications of Electrolysis
topics.notesHtml:
Applications of Electrolysis

1. Purification of Metals

When metals are extracted from their ore, they are often not very pure. Electrolysis can be used to purify them (electrolytic purification).

At the anode: the (impure) copper anode dissolves to form copper ions: Cu (s) → Cu²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻. Impurities that are more reactive than hydrogen dissolve into the solution, while less reactive impurities sink and are deposited at the bottom.

At the cathode: pure copper is deposited on the cathode: Cu²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu (s).

Observations:

  • The CuSO₄ solution remains the same blue colour and concentration, as for every copper ion lost at the cathode (to coat the object), one copper ion is released at the anode — so the concentration of copper ions in the solution remains the same throughout and the solution does not become more pale.
  • The anode dissolves and decreases in size as usual.
  • The cathode increases in size with a copper coating.

2. Electroplating

Electroplating: the process of depositing a layer of metal onto another substance using electrolysis. It is useful for giving a good decorative finish to objects and can also form a protective layer that prevents metals from corrosion.

At the anode: the copper anode dissolves to form copper ions: Cu (s) → Cu²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻.

At the cathode: copper forms a layer around the object: Cu²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu (s).

Observations:

  • The CuSO₄ solution remains the same blue colour and concentration, as for every copper ion lost at the cathode to coat the object, one copper ion is released at the anode — so the concentration of copper ions in the solution remains the same throughout and the solution does not become more pale.
  • The anode dissolves and decreases in size as usual.

topics.title: Simple Cells
topics.notesHtml:
Simple Cells

Simple Cell / Voltaic Cell: a device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy. It is also known as an electric cell.

A simple cell is made by placing two different metals in contact with an electrolyte. The metals act as electrodes for the simple cell. Electrons flow from the more reactive metal to the less reactive metal. Since electrons flow from the more reactive metal, it becomes the negative electrode, and the less reactive metal becomes the positive electrode.

At the zinc electrode (anode): Zn dissolves (oxidises) to form Zn²⁺ ions: Zn (s) → Zn²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻

At the copper electrode (cathode): copper ions in the solution receive electrons and reduce to form copper: Cu²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu (s)

Overall reaction: Zn (s) + Cu²⁺ (aq) → Zn²⁺ (aq) + Cu (s)

shortAnswer.prompt: Describe how a simple cell made of zinc and copper electrodes generates electricity, including the half-equations at each electrode.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: A simple cell is made by placing zinc and copper electrodes in contact with an electrolyte. Since zinc is more reactive than copper, electrons flow from zinc to copper through the external circuit. At the zinc electrode (anode), zinc atoms lose electrons to form Zn²⁺ ions: Zn (s) → Zn²⁺ (aq) + 2e⁻. topics.title: Speed of Reaction
topics.notesHtml:
Speed of Reaction

When chemicals react, different reactions take place at different speeds. Some reactions are very fast (e.g. explosion of a petrol–air mixture, or precipitation of AgCl from NaCl(aq) and AgNO₃), while others are moderately fast (e.g. reaction of calcium with water) or slow (e.g. rusting of iron in air, or fermentation).

Speed of Reaction: tells us how fast or slow a reaction takes place.

Measuring Speed of Reaction

In a laboratory experiment, the speed of a reaction can be found through either:

1. Measuring the Amount of Product Formed in a Certain Time (per unit time)

Speed of Reaction = Amount of Product formed / time taken

Example — reaction of Mg and HCl: Mg (s) + HCl (aq) → MgCl (aq) + H₂ (g)

Gas produced during a reaction can be measured using:

  • Lime water (if CO₂ is produced)
  • Gas syringe (also used to find moles of gas)
  • Gas pressure sensor

Using a gas syringe, the volume of gas produced is measured at regular intervals to find the speed of the reaction.

Note: If the reaction is too fast and the gas syringe fills before sufficient measurements can be made, dilute the reactant to slow it down and monitor.

The change in the gradient of a volume-against-time graph tells us the change in the speed of reaction:

  • At the beginning, the gradient is steepest — this means the reaction is fastest, due to the greatest concentration of reactants.
  • As more reactants are used up, the gradient becomes less steep (gentler) as the reaction slows down.
  • Eventually, the gradient reaches 0 as all reactants are used up and the reaction stops.
2. Measuring the Amount of Reactant(s) Used Up in a Certain Time (per unit time)

Speed of Reaction = Amount of Reactant used up / time taken

Example — reaction of marble chips (CaCO₃) and HCl: 2HCl (aq) + CaCO₃ (s) → CaCl₂ (aq) + CO₂ (g) + H₂O (l)

Note: A thread is used so that the total mass of the setup can be recorded before the reaction starts; this results in a less delayed reaction and less wastage.

Factors Affecting Speed of Reaction

Collision Theory

The Collision Theory states that the rate of a chemical reaction is proportional to the number of collisions between reactant molecules. The more often reactant molecules collide, the more often they react with one another and the faster the rate of reaction.

Effective collisions are collisions that result in the formation of products. In order to produce effective collisions, reactant particles must possess some minimum amount of energy. This energy, used to initiate the reaction, is called the activation energy.

For an effective collision (chemical reaction) to occur:

  1. Reactants must collide with each other.
  2. Molecules must have sufficient energy to initiate the reaction (activation energy).
  3. Molecules must have the proper orientation.
Factors and Their Effects
FactorEffect
1. TemperatureAt low temperatures, reactant particles move slowly because they have little energy. When temperature increases, particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so collisions between particles are more frequent and there is a higher frequency of effective collisions. Therefore the speed of reaction increases. (↑ Temperature → ↑ KE → ↑ Frequency of effective collisions → ↑ Speed of reaction)
2. Particle SizeWhen particle size decreases, there is a greater surface area to volume ratio, so collisions between particles are more frequent and there is a higher frequency of effective collisions. Therefore the speed of reaction increases. (↓ Particle size → ↑ Surface area to volume ratio → ↑ Frequency of effective collisions → ↑ Speed of reaction)
3. ConcentrationWhen concentration increases, there are more particles occupying a given volume (i.e. more moles per dm³ of reactants), so collisions between particles are more frequent and there is a higher frequency of effective collisions. Therefore the speed of reaction increases. (↑ Concentration → ↑ mol/dm³ → ↑ Frequency of effective collisions → ↑ Speed of reaction)
4. Pressure (Gases) — similar to concentrationWhen the pressure of a gaseous reactant is higher, reacting gas particles are closer together, so collisions between particles are more frequent and there is a higher frequency of effective collisions. Therefore the speed of reaction increases. (↑ Pressure of gas → Gas particles closer together → ↑ Frequency of effective collisions → ↑ Speed of reaction)

Comparing Graphs of Speed of Reactions

Using the setup of CaCO₃ and HCl: (1) measure CO₂ produced at regular intervals; (2) repeat using setups with a changed variable (temperature, particle size, concentration).

The steeper the initial gradient, the higher the speed of reaction. The higher the concentration/temperature/surface area, the faster the speed of reaction and the shorter it takes for the reaction to be completed.

Both graphs also show the reaction slowing down over time as the reactants are used up (concentration of HCl and mass of CaCO₃ decreases). Both graphs show that the reaction stops when 100 cm³ of CO₂ is collected.

CaCO₃ : HCl molar ratio = 1 : 2, i.e. 0.01 : 0.02 mol.

Since CaCO₃ is the limiting reagent, and the same mass of CaCO₃ is used in both experiments, changing the concentration of HCl (i.e. moles of HCl) does not change the molar ratio and volume of CO₂ collected.

topics.title: Effects of Catalysts and Enzymes
topics.notesHtml:
Effects of Catalysts and Enzymes

The speed of a reaction can be increased by adding a catalyst.

A catalyst:

  • Increases the speed of a reaction
  • Remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction

Characteristics of catalysts:

  • Only changes the speed and not the yield of a chemical reaction
  • Only a small amount is needed to change the speed of the reaction
  • Not used up during the reaction; the same amount is present at the beginning and the end of a reaction
  • Physical appearance may change (NOT mass) at the end of a reaction, but chemical properties remain unchanged
  • Lowers the activation energy of a reaction
  • Selective in its action; different catalysts speed up different reactions
  • Impurities can prevent it from working; the catalyst is said to be poisoned/inactivated by impurities

Catalyst: A substance that increases the speed of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway for the reaction to proceed. The catalysed reaction has a lower activation energy than the reaction without the catalyst.

Notes for Examinations

  • When the question requires you to label a graph, always label the axes.
  • When given data and asked to refer to it, answer as such: "In the first 5 min, the volume of CO2 produced is ___ while in the next 5 min, the volume produced is less at ____, showing …"
  • Always include frequency of effective collisions increasing/decreasing when answering questions on factors affecting rate of reaction.

topics.notesHtml:
Energy Changes

Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions

ExothermicEndothermic
Raise in temperature, e.g. 28°C to 34°C. Heat is transferred from the reactants to the surroundings, causing the temperature to rise and the container to feel hot. Reactions that give out heat energy to the surroundings.Drop in temperature, e.g. 28°C to 22°C. Heat is transferred from the surroundings to the reactants, causing the temperature to drop and the container to feel cooler. Reactions that absorb heat energy from the surroundings.
Examples: Dissolving anhydrous salts (e.g. anhydrous Na2CO3, anhydrous CuSO4) in water; Neutralisation; Dissolving of concentrated H2SO4 in water; Combustion of fuels (wood, coal, petroleum, natural gas); Corrosion of metals (e.g. rusting of iron); Respiration; CondensationExamples: Dissolving some ionic compounds (e.g. NH4Cl, Na2CO3 crystals) in water; Thermal decomposition (CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, with heat); Photosynthesis (6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2); Action of light on AgBr in photographic film; Evaporation

All reactions involve either the breaking of bonds of reactants or the forming of bonds of products, or both.

Bond MakingBond Breaking
Energy is released during bond making. Since energy is given out, bond making is exothermic.Energy is required to break bonds. Since energy is taken in, bond breaking is endothermic.
Particles lose heat energy to the surroundings, they vibrate slower and the forces of attraction between particles increase. topics.title: Heat Changes in a Reaction
topics.notesHtml:
Heat Changes in a Reaction

The amount of energy involved in a reaction is known as the heat change or enthalpy change of the reaction. This is measured in kilojoules (kJ) and represented by ΔH. (Δ = Change; H = Heat/Energy content)

ΔH = Total energy of products − Total energy of reactants

ExothermicEndothermic
ΔH is negative (<0) as chemicals have lost energy to the surroundings, thus the energy content of products is lower than reactants.ΔH is positive (>0) as chemicals have gained energy from the surroundings, thus the energy content of products is higher than reactants.

Bond breaking (in reactants) and bond making (to form products) occurs in chemical reactions. To identify if a reaction is exothermic or endothermic, the enthalpy change of the overall reaction is derived from the enthalpy change of bond breaking and bond making.

Worked example: 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g)

  • Energy required to break 1 mol of H-H bonds: 436 kJ
  • Energy required to break 1 mol of O=O bonds: 496 kJ
  • Energy released on forming 1 mol of O-H bonds: 463 kJ
  • 1 mol of H2O has 2 O-H bonds, so 2 mol of H2O has 4 O-H bonds
  • Total energy absorbed for bond breaking: 2(436) + 496 = 1368 kJ
  • Total energy released for bond making: 4(463) = 1852 kJ
  • ΔH reaction = 1368 − 1852 = −484 kJ

This means the energy absorbed in breaking the bonds in 2 moles of H2 gas (H-H) and 1 mole of O2 gas (O=O) is less than the energy released in forming the bonds in 2 moles of H2O (O-H). Hence the reaction is exothermic.

Note: The number of bonds broken or formed does not tell whether a reaction is exothermic; only the energy that is released or absorbed does so. If reactions are more complicated, it is good to redraw the molecules using line (structural) diagrams to make the bonds clearer, e.g. CH4(g) + Cl2(g) → CH3Cl(g) + HCl(g).

topics.notesHtml:
Activation Energy and Energy Profile Diagrams

Activation Energy, Ea: the minimum amount of energy that reactant particles must possess in order for a chemical reaction to occur.

All reactions need energy to get started. Heat provides the energy to change less energetic particles into more energetic particles, starting the reaction. Therefore, the activation energy acts as an energy barrier that must be overcome by the reactants before they can react to form products, i.e. the reaction will only occur when reactant particles possess energy equal to or more than the activation energy Ea:

  • When reactant particles have energy < Ea: No reaction occurs
  • When reactant particles have energy > Ea: Chemical reaction occurs

Energy profile diagrams illustrate the change in energy in the reactants and products as the reaction progresses. They also show the enthalpy change (ΔH) and the activation energy.

topics.title: Combustion of Fuels
topics.notesHtml:
Combustion of Fuels

Fuels: Substances that can burn easily in air to give out energy (e.g. coal, petroleum, natural gas, wood).

A complete combustion (excess air) has products carbon dioxide and water (depending on the reactant):

  • C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g) + heat energy
  • CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + H2O(l) + heat energy

An incomplete combustion has products carbon monoxide, water and carbon:

  • 4CH4(g) + 5O2(g) → 2CO(g) + 8H2O(l) + 2C(s) + heat energy

In a fuel cell, reactants are continuously supplied to produce electricity directly. The best-known example, the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, is used as a source of electrical power in space vehicles:

  • At cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e− → 4OH−
  • At anode: 2H2 + 4OH− → 4H2O + 4e−
  • Overall: O2 + 2H2 → 2H2O

Unlike chemical cells (batteries), reactants are not contained in the cell but are instead continuously supplied from an external reservoir.

Advantages of Fuel CellsDisadvantages of Fuel Cells
Renewable energy source; Pollution-free because only water is produced; Hydrogen is an efficient source of energy, providing twice the amount of energy compared to many other fuels; Less wastage of energy compared to combustionIt is difficult to find a cheap source of hydrogen – obtaining hydrogen from electrolysis is an expensive process; Hydrogen is extremely flammable and explosive, so special precautions must be taken in the storage and transport of the gas; Hydrogen is very light, and thus requires larger storage volumes compared to other fuels

topics.title: Organic Chemistry: Introduction and Production of Fuels and Hydrocarbons
topics.notesHtml:
Organic Chemistry

All organic compounds contain carbon, and most also contain hydrogen. Some organic compounds may also have oxygen, halogen and nitrogen atoms. This does not mean all carbon-containing compounds are organic (CO2, CO, diamond/graphite, carbonates and carbides are all examples of inorganic compounds).

Hydrocarbons: Organic compounds that contain only hydrogen and carbon atoms.

Production of Fuels and Hydrocarbons

Hydrocarbons are primarily made from petroleum and natural gas (sources of energy).

  • Petroleum: a mixture of hydrocarbons (mainly alkanes), also known as crude oil.
  • Natural Gas: about 70 to 90% methane, and about 0 to 20% other short-chain alkanes such as ethane, propane and butane.

Petroleum and natural gas are extracted by oil rigs and refineries in the ocean, from deep under the ocean floor where sea animals and plants decomposed due to heat and pressure from the Earth over time, thus forming petroleum and natural gas.

In order to produce various fuels and hydrocarbons, crude oil undergoes fractional distillation.

topics.title: Competing Uses of Petroleum
topics.notesHtml:
Competing Uses of Petroleum

Petroleum is a non-renewable resource. This means that the supply of petroleum is limited.

In order to conserve petroleum:

  • Reduce the number of motor vehicles on the road by taking public transport such as buses and the MRT.
  • Drive cars that consume less petrol (e.g. electric cars).
  • Improve the design of power stations and vehicles for more efficient use of petroleum.
  • Use alternative energy sources such as solar energy and nuclear energy.
  • Use alternative fuels, such as:
    • Biofuel (e.g. biogas, produced when dead plants or animals decay in the absence of air, or biodiesel, made from plant oils like palm oil)
    • Gasohol (a mixture of ethanol and petrol)

The Homologous Series

Related organic compounds are grouped together in families called homologous series. These include alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids.

Homologous Series: A family of organic compounds with:

  • Same functional group
  • Similar chemical properties
  • A gradual change in their physical properties down the series
  • Same general formula

Functional Group: An atom or group of atoms that gives a molecule its characteristic properties.

topics.title: Naming Organic Compounds
topics.notesHtml:
Naming Organic Compounds

The names of organic compounds can be split into 2 parts:

  1. Prefix shows the number of carbon atoms in one molecule
  2. Suffix shows the homologous series the compound belongs to
Number of Carbon atomsPrefix
1Meth-
2Eth-
3Prop-
4But-
5Pent-
6Hex-
7Hept-
8Oct-
9Non-
10Dec-
SuffixHomologous Series
-aneAlkane
-eneAlkene
-olAlcohol
-oic acidCarboxylic Acid

Note: Since alkenes consist of a C=C double bond, there is no such thing as "methene".

Branched Carbon Chains

For non-straight carbon chains, the alkyl group will appear in the name. For example, 2-methylpropane is an isomer of butane.

The carbon chain should be rearranged such that branches form out of the longest possible chain. For example, a compound that at first glance may seem to be "2-ethylpropane" is actually wrong: when rewritten with the longest carbon chain, it becomes a 4-carbon chain with a methyl group attached to the 2nd carbon, i.e. 2-methylbutane.

Functional Groups and Isomer Naming

For certain homologous series, the placement of the functional group produces different compounds with the same molecular formula (isomers). This applies to alcohols as well as alkenes, where the number represents the carbon atom which the double bond starts from (e.g. but-1-ene has its double bond at the end while but-2-ene has it in the centre).

Addition of Halogens

With the addition/substitution of halogens, the name of the resultant compound will start with the position of the halogen atoms in relation to the carbon atoms, followed by the prefix (di, tri, tetra, etc.) chloro/bromo/fluoro and the alkane name.

For the combination of the above naming rules, the halogen is named first, followed by the alkyl branch and the functional group, e.g. 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

Isomers: Compounds which share the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. Isomers have different physical properties (e.g. melting point, boiling point) but chemically behave in the same way.

topics.title: Alkanes
topics.notesHtml:
Alkanes

Alkanes: Hydrocarbons that contain only carbon-carbon single covalent bonds (saturated hydrocarbons).

General Formula: CnH2n+2. Each member of the alkane family differs from the next by a -CH2- unit.

Number of C atomsAlkaneMolecular Formula
1MethaneCH4
2EthaneC2H6
3PropaneC3H8
4ButaneC4H10

Isomerism in Alkanes

From butane onwards, other than the typical straight carbon chains, alkanes can also form isomers with alkyl groups.

Alkyl groups have the general formula CnH2n+1 and include: Methyl (CH3-), Ethyl (CH3CH2-), Propyl (CH3CH2CH2-), Butyl (CH3CH2CH2CH2-).

Take butane (C4H10) as an example: other than the 4-carbon straight chain, it can form a 3-carbon chain with a methyl branch from the central carbon (2-methylpropane).

Pentane (C5H12) has 3 isomers:

  • Pentane, C5H12 – 5-carbon chain (longest)
  • 2-methylbutane – 4-carbon chain with a methyl group attached to the 2nd carbon atom
  • 2,2-dimethylpropane – 3-carbon chain with 2 methyl groups attached to the 2nd carbon atom

To find isomers, systematically remove a CH3 group (methyl group) from the end of the chain and see where else it can fit in place of one of the other hydrogens (the hydrogen joins the carbon atom that the methyl group came from).

Note: It may seem possible to form another isomer using an ethyl group on a 3-carbon chain, but as stated before, the longest chain must be used – this is actually a 4-carbon chain with a methyl group attached to the 2nd carbon, i.e. 2-methylbutane. When working with structural isomers, always ensure the longest chain is drawn horizontal.

Physical Properties of Alkanes

  • Low melting point (MPT) and boiling point (BPT); the first 4 members in the series exist as gases at room temperature and pressure (rtp)
  • Insoluble in water
  • Soluble in organic solvents

Down the series: molecular size increases, intermolecular forces of attraction (IMFOA) between alkane molecules increase, and more energy is required to overcome the IMFOA between molecules. Thus, down the series:

  1. MPT and BPT of alkanes increase
  2. Alkanes become more viscous (flow less easily)
  3. Flammability decreases – percentage of carbon increases, making the alkane harder to burn and producing a smokier flame

Chemical Properties of Alkanes

1. Combustion

Alkanes burn in excess air (oxygen) to produce CO2 and H2O vapour. If oxygen is limited, H2O will still form along with CO and C (as soot). CO is odourless, colourless and poisonous, hence dangerous, as it interferes with the way oxygen is carried around the body. The reaction is highly exothermic (produces a lot of heat), hence alkanes are used as fuels.

  • Complete: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + H2O(l) + heat energy
  • Incomplete: 4CH4(g) + 5O2(g) → 2CO(g) + 8H2O(l) + 2C(s) + heat energy

2. Substitution Reaction

Substitution reactions occur when an atom in a molecule is replaced by a different atom. Alkanes react with halogens (Cl2, Br2, etc.) in the presence of UV light, which triggers the reaction by splitting the Cl2 or Br2 molecules into individual atoms.

For the reaction between methane and chlorine gas, a colourless gas, chloromethane (CH3Cl), is produced along with fumes of HCl gas. A similar reaction occurs with Br2 instead of Cl2, producing bromomethane and hydrogen bromide.

With successive reactions, more hydrogen atoms in the alkane are replaced by chlorine atoms, until all hydrogen atoms are substituted. Note that the reaction cannot result in H2 gas produced and 2 chlorine atoms substituted into the alkane in one step – dichloroalkanes form via successive reactions.

For reactions involving larger alkanes, the placement of halogen atoms may affect the product achieved. With propane, the hydrogen replaced could be at either the middle or end of the chain, so 2 different molecules may be formed from the substitution of chlorine:

  • 1-chloropropane: CH3CH2CH2Cl
  • 2-chloropropane: CH3CHClCH3

topics.title: Alkenes
topics.notesHtml:
Alkenes

Alkenes: Hydrocarbons that contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds (unsaturated hydrocarbons).

General Formula: CnH2n. Each member of the alkene family differs from the next by a -CH2- unit. Functional group: C=C.

Number of C atomsAlkeneMolecular Formula
2EtheneC2H4
3PropeneC3H6
4ButeneC4H8

Isomerism in Alkenes

Similar to alkanes, from butene onwards, alkenes can form isomers with alkyl groups. As seen from the naming of organic compounds, alkenes also form isomers depending on where the functional group (C=C bond) starts. Butene, C4H8, has 3 isomers.

Physical Properties of Alkenes

Physical properties of alkenes are similar to those of alkanes:

  • Low MPT and BPT (the first 3 in the series exist as gases at rtp)
  • Insoluble in water
  • Soluble in organic solvents

Down the series: molecular size increases, IMFOA between alkene molecules increases, and more energy is required to overcome the IMFOA between molecules. Thus, down the series: MPT and BPT increase, alkenes become more viscous (flow less easily), and flammability decreases as percentage of carbon increases (harder to burn, smokier flame produced).

Chemical Properties of Alkenes

1. Combustion

Alkenes burn in excess air (oxygen) to produce CO2 and H2O vapour. As alkenes contain a higher percentage of carbon (being unsaturated) than the corresponding alkanes, incomplete combustion is more likely. Hence they burn with a sootier flame (carbon is 81.8% of propane but 85.7% of propene).

C2H4(g) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(g) (with heat)

2. Addition Reaction

The carbon-carbon double bonds (C=C) in alkenes are very reactive. Due to the property of its functional group, alkenes readily undergo addition reactions, in which an unsaturated organic compound combines with another substance to form a new single compound.

  • a. Hydrogenation: Addition of H2 to alkenes to form alkanes. Conditions: 200°C, nickel catalyst. Note: this reaction may seem pointless as ethene is a very useful compound used to make many things, while ethane is only a fuel.
  • b. Bromination: Addition of Br2 to alkenes. This reaction is used to test for the presence of unsaturated hydrocarbons and can be used to distinguish between an alkane and an alkene. Bromine water is used instead of the dangerous liquid bromine.
    AlkaneAlkene
    Ethane does not decolourise bromine solution under normal conditions. Bromine remains reddish-brown.Ethene decolourises the solution. Bromine solution turns from reddish-brown to colourless.
  • c. Hydration: Addition of steam (H2O) to alkenes to form alcohols. Conditions: 300°C, 60 atm, phosphoric(V) acid catalyst (H3PO4).

3. Addition Polymerisation

Reaction between alkene molecules (monomers) to form a long molecule (polymer). Conditions: high temperature and pressure, catalyst. (More on polymerisation is covered under macromolecules.)

Production of Alkenes

Cracking: Breaking down of long-chain hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons or hydrogen.

Alkenes are obtained by cracking petroleum. For example, nonane can be broken down to form heptane and ethene: C9H20 → C7H16 + C2H4.

Breaking the long hydrocarbon chain produces 2 fragments, but these fragments are not viable on their own and need some rearrangement of hydrogen atoms – a hydrogen atom from the far-right CH3 is transferred to the CH2 on the left-hand fragment.

The nonane molecule can also break at different points to produce other fragments, e.g. C9H20 → C6H14 + C3H6.

Industrial Catalytic CrackingCracking in the School Lab
In catalytic cracking, a catalyst is used to speed up the process of cracking. Conditions: high temperature (e.g. 600°C), aluminium oxide (Al2O3) and silicon dioxide (SiO2) catalysts.

Importance of Cracking

  1. Production of short-chain alkenes, e.g. C18H38 → C6H14 + 6C2H4. Short-chain alkenes like ethene and propene are extremely useful and can be used to make ethanol and plastics.
  2. Production of hydrogen, e.g. C18H38 → C8H16 + C10H20 + H2. Hydrogen is used in the manufacture of ammonia, which is used to make fertilisers.
  3. Converting hydrocarbons of higher molecular mass into smaller molecules which are in higher demand – for example, there is a higher demand for petrol than lubricating oil or diesel oil. Petrol can be obtained through catalytic cracking of diesel and lubricating oils.

Alkanes vs Alkenes

Both are hydrocarbons; both are flammable and burn completely in excess oxygen to produce CO2 and H2O.

AlkanesAlkenes
Contain only C-C (single) bondsContain one or more C=C (double) bonds
Generally unreactiveVery reactive
Undergo substitution reactions; do not react with aqueous bromine under normal conditions (requires UV light and time)Undergo addition reactions; rapidly decolourise aqueous bromine
Produce a less smoky flame than an alkene with the same number of carbon atomsProduce a smokier flame than an alkane with the same number of carbon atoms
Do not undergo polymerisationUndergo addition polymerisation
