topics.title: Alcohols
topics.notesHtml:
Alcohols

Alcohols: Series of organic compounds which have the hydroxyl (-OH) functional group.

General Formula: CnH2n+1OH. Functional group: -OH.

Number of C atomsAlcoholMolecular Formula
1MethanolCH3OH
2EthanolC2H5OH
3PropanolC3H7OH
4ButanolC4H9OH

Physical Properties of Alcohols

Alcohols are volatile liquids at rtp. Down the series: molecular size increases, IMFOA increases, solubility of alcohols decreases, and BPT of alcohols increases.

AlcoholPhysical StateSolubility in WaterBoiling Point (°C)
MethanolLiquidVery Soluble65
EthanolLiquidVery Soluble78
PropanolLiquidSoluble97
ButanolLiquidSlightly Soluble118

Chemical Properties of Alcohols

1. Combustion

Alcohols burn in excess air (oxygen) to produce carbon dioxide and water vapour: C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O. This reaction is highly exothermic (produces a lot of heat), hence alcohols are used as fuels.

2. Oxidation

Alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids when heated with oxidising agents such as acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO4 (or potassium dichromate(VI), K2Cr2O7).

Conditions: excess of oxidising agent; heat the mixture for a long time.

If KMnO4 is used as the oxidising agent, the colour of the solution will change from purple to colourless (note: if KMnO4 is added in excess, the colour will not turn colourless but instead remain a light purple).

Breathalysers

The police use breathalysers to test the amount of alcohol consumed by drivers. It contains an oxidising agent, usually acidified potassium dichromate, and a catalyst. A colour change is registered if a certain amount of alcohol is present in the breath.

Production of Ethanol

1. Catalytic Addition of Steam to Ethene

Conditions: 300°C, 60 atm, phosphoric(V) acid catalyst (H3PO4).

2. Fermentation of Carbohydrates

Alcohol fermentation occurs when a microorganism such as yeast acts on carbohydrates (glucose, fructose, sucrose) in anaerobic conditions (absence of oxygen) to produce ethanol and CO2.

In the laboratory, glucose solution is mixed with yeast and kept at 37°C. Carbon dioxide produced during fermentation forms a white precipitate in limewater.

A dilute solution of ethanol (15% alcohol) is produced. A higher alcohol content is not produced as it causes the yeast to die and fermentation to stop. Ethanol can be extracted by fractional distillation. This allows for higher concentrations of alcoholic beverages or pure ethanol to be produced.

Precautions:

  • Fermentation only takes place in anaerobic conditions, hence the flask must be tightly stoppered.
  • Limewater is used as an air lock.
  • Temperature should be kept at 37°C or the enzymes will be denatured and fermentation will stop.

When wine or beer is left exposed to air in the open for a few days, it turns sour. Ethanol undergoes oxidation to form ethanoic acid (vinegar); thus fermentation of carbohydrates only takes place in the absence of oxygen.

Uses of Ethanol

  • In alcoholic drinks (beer, wine, rum, sake)
  • As a solvent in paints, varnishes, deodorants, perfumes, colognes
  • As a fuel in cars (often mixed with petrol)
  • As a fuel for cooking

topics.title: Carboxylic Acids
topics.notesHtml:
Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic Acids: Series of organic acids which have the carboxyl (-COOH) functional group.

General Formula: CnH2n+1COOH (note: since the functional group already contains a C, methanoic acid starts from n=0). Functional group: -COOH.

Number of C atomsCarboxylic AcidFormula
1Methanoic AcidHCOOH
2Ethanoic AcidCH3COOH
3Propanoic AcidC2H5COOH
4Butanoic AcidC3H7COOH

Physical Properties of Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids are very soluble in water and exist as colourless liquids at rtp. Their boiling points are above that of water and increase down the series (with increasing molecular size).

Carboxylic acids are weak acids as they ionise partially in water, i.e. low concentration of H+ ions (pH 5-6). Due to the hydrogen ions produced, carboxylic acids have acidic properties.

The CH3COO- ions are called ethanoate ions. Due to the structure of ethanoate (or any other ion from a carboxylic acid), cations are attracted to the O- in the anion. Hence salts formed are written as, e.g., (CH3COO)2Mg – this keeps the structure of the compound more understandable, instead of writing Mg(OOCCH3)2.

Chemical Properties of Carboxylic Acids

1. Simple Acid Reactions

  • a. Reaction with Reactive Metals: Like all acids, metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series will react with carboxylic acids. Carboxylic Acid + Metal → Salt + Hydrogen. E.g. 2CH3COOH(aq) + Mg(s) → (CH3COO)2Mg(aq) + H2(g)
  • b. Reaction with Carbonates: carboxylic acid + carbonate → salt + carbon dioxide + water
  • c. Reaction with Bases: carboxylic acid + base → salt + water
  • d. Esterification: Carboxylic acids react with alcohols under certain conditions to produce a new compound called an ester. carboxylic acid + alcohol → ester + water

Production of Ethanoic Acid

1. Oxidation of Ethanol with Acidified KMnO4

Potassium manganate(VII) acts as an oxidising agent and is reduced. Its colour changes from purple to colourless. Since ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid, ethanol acts as a reducing agent.

2. Oxidation of Ethanol by Atmospheric Oxygen

Certain bacteria in the air oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid. Thus, alcoholic drinks turn sour when left exposed to air for a few days.

topics.title: Esters
topics.notesHtml:
Esters

Esters: An organic compound derived from carboxylic acids with the -COO- functional group.

  • Sweet-smelling, colourless liquids that are insoluble in water
  • Contain the -COO- functional group
  • Formed by the reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, also known as esterification

Esterification

Conditions: warmed, with a few drops of concentrated H2SO4 as catalyst.

  • A warm water bath is used instead of a direct flame, as all the organic components of the mixture are flammable; ethyl ethanoate also has a low boiling point.
  • The ester is poured into cold water after the reaction, as everything else in the mixture dissolves in water, leaving the insoluble ester layer which can be smelt (this gets rid of the strong smell of the ethanoic acid).

For example, ethanoic acid and ethanol react in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form water and an ester called ethyl ethanoate. The -OH in ethanoic acid is replaced by the -C2H5O from ethanol, and joins the remaining H to form water.

Naming Esters

The name of an ester consists of 2 parts: the first part is derived from the alcohol, and the second part is derived from the carboxylic acid.

Uses of Esters

  • In the preparation of perfumes
  • As artificial food flavourings
  • As solvents for cosmetics and glues
  • In soaps – naturally-occurring esters such as animal fats and vegetable oils are boiled with sodium hydroxide to form soap

topics.title: Macromolecules and Polymerisation
topics.notesHtml:
Macromolecules

Macromolecule: A very large molecule made up of many small molecules.

A polymer is a type of long-chain macromolecule that is covalently linked together by many small repeat units called monomers. Different polymers are made up of different monomers.

Natural PolymersSynthetic Polymers
Proteins, DNA, Starch, Cellulose, Wool, Natural rubber, SilkPoly(ethene), Nylon, Terylene, Polyvinyl chloride (PVC), Polyvinyl acetate (PVA), Teflon, Polystyrene

Polymerisation: Process of joining together a large number of monomers to form a polymer. There are 2 types of polymerisation: Addition Polymerisation and Condensation Polymerisation.

Addition Polymerisation

Addition Polymerisation: When monomer units join together without losing any molecules or atoms.

Alkenes have reactive C=C bonds, hence can undergo addition polymerisation.

Conditions (not definite; differs based on type of polymer and polymer length): high pressure (e.g. 1000 atm), high temperature (e.g. 200°C), catalyst.

Example: Ethene → Poly(ethene). The formula of the polymer can be written using its repeat unit. The letter 'n' represents a large number of repeat units. The number of ethene molecules in each poly(ethene) molecule varies between 10,000 and 30,000.

Deducing the Structural Formula of a Polymer/Monomer

  1. Given a monomer, e.g. propene, C3H6, and asked to draw a length of poly(propene) chain: draw the given monomer such that all the attachments are kept out of the way of the C=C bond, then derive the repeat unit by splitting the double bond, then draw the required length of chain, ensuring extension bonds are included to show that the polymer extends beyond the drawn chain.
  2. Given a polymer, e.g. PVA (polyvinyl acetate), and asked to draw the structural formula of the monomer: identify and write down the formula of the repeat unit, then convert the C-C single bond into a C=C double bond, giving the structural formula of the monomer.

Uses of Addition Polymers

Addition polymers are good insulators of heat and electricity, and are resistant to chemical attack.

  • Poly(ethene) can be easily moulded into different shapes. It is used to make plastic toys, clingfilm, plastic bags, and buckets.
  • Polystyrene is hard, light and brittle. It is used to make disposable containers.
  • Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is used to make pipes, raincoats, flooring mats and thin gloves.
  • Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene) is used in 'non-stick' frying pans.
  • Perspex is used for the windscreens of cars.

Condensation Polymerisation

Condensation Polymerisation: When monomer units join together to form a polymer with the loss/removal of a small molecule (e.g. water).

Condensation polymers are made from two different monomers with a functional group at each end of each monomer, thus giving the polymer a linkage of its own. This linkage depends on the type of condensation polymer. There are two types of condensation polymers: polyamides and polyesters.

Polyamides

The monomers of polyamides (e.g. Nylon) are a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine.

  • Dicarboxylic acid: any acid with a carboxyl (-COOH) functional group at both ends of the molecule (2 functional groups – "di"), joined together by any hydrocarbon (represented by a rectangle).
  • Diamine: any amine with an amine functional group (-NH2) at both ends of the molecule (2 functional groups – "di"), joined together by any hydrocarbon (represented by a rectangle).

When a dicarboxylic acid is reacted with a diamine, the breaking of C-O bonds and N-H bonds occurs to form water, which is removed. The repeat unit of a polyamide contains the amide linkage (-CONH-), as suggested by the name "polyamide".

Polyesters

The monomers of polyesters (e.g. Terylene) are a dicarboxylic acid and a diol.

  • Dicarboxylic acid: any acid with a carboxyl (-COOH) functional group at both ends of the molecule (2 functional groups – "di"), joined together by any hydrocarbon (represented by a rectangle).
  • Diol: any alcohol with a hydroxyl functional group (-OH) at both ends of the molecule (2 functional groups – "di"), joined together by any hydrocarbon (represented by a rectangle).

When a dicarboxylic acid is reacted with a diol, the breaking of C-O bonds and O-H bonds occurs to form water, which is removed. The repeat unit of a polyester contains the ester linkage (-COO-), as suggested by the name "polyester".

Uses of Man-made Fibres

  • Synthetic or man-made fibres are usually plastics which have been spun into threads.
  • Terylene and nylon are the best-known examples of synthetic fibres.
  • Clothes made from these fibres are shrink-proof and crease-proof. They are also easier to wash and dry.
  • Examples of items made from nylon and Terylene include curtains, parachutes, fishing lines and sleeping bags.

Advantages and Disadvantages of Plastics

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Easily moulded into various shapes; Light, tough and waterproof; Durable (note: do not say "cheap" or "relatively cheap")Land Pollution: Plastics are non-biodegradable (do not break down and decompose easily) and are not decomposed by bacteria in the soil, leading to a build-up of waste.
Air Pollution: Plastics are flammable. When plastics burn, fires can spread very quickly and poisonous gases are produced.
Water Pollution: Plastics thrown into the sea endanger marine animals, which mistake plastics for food and choke on them. Plastics can also clog up rivers and drains, which may become breeding grounds for mosquitoes.
